## This is a different kind of task {.smaller}

- The other 8 services' InVEST runs were done by you and collaborators, earlier, separately — this project only ever **post-processed** the finished outputs
- **Nobody has run InVEST SWY globally before** — on this project, or (as far as this review found) anywhere — precisely because a single global calibration isn't considered defensible
- This week was a **literature review and specification**, not a build: what a real global run requires, what already exists, what's been de-risked, what's still open

::: {.notes}
Open with this before anything else — make sure the scope shift lands before diving into content. This isn't "add a table to the pipeline," it's standing up and running a real model for the first time on this project. Don't undersell it, don't oversell it either — just be accurate about what kind of task this is.
:::

## No global precedent — but a major shortcut exists {.smaller}

- No published global-scale InVEST SWY application found anywhere. Closest: Hamel et al. 2020, Peru + Myanmar (*J. Environ. Manage.* 270:110792) — multi-region, not global. **Full text now obtained and read** (not just abstract-level)
- Checked SWAT's global databases as a possible curve-number shortcut — **ruled out**: they only crosswalk land cover to SWAT's own crop codes, no CN values
- Found **GCN250** (Jaafar et al. 2019): a global 250m gridded curve-number product — not InVEST-specific, but solves the same underlying problem (CN varies by land cover and place, no single number works everywhere)

::: {.notes}
Checking SWAT and ruling it out was a real, useful step — confirms there's no existing shortcut in that ecosystem either, not just an unchecked assumption.

Hamel et al. 2020 turned out to matter more than expected once read in full — it doesn't just confirm precedent, it changes two things covered on the next two slides.
:::

## What Hamel et al. 2020 actually changes {.smaller}

- **Neither of their case studies derived CN/Kc from literature tables cold.** Peru reused CN from an existing *calibrated SWAT model* of that exact basin. Myanmar reused CN/Kc from an existing *national ecosystem-service assessment* (Mandle et al. 2017)
- **This answers "how do we build subregional tables"**: search for an existing calibrated study covering a representative watershed in each flagged biome, don't derive from TR-55 tables cold
- **CN sensitivity is dramatic, not theoretical**: their own test found quickflow changed by **10.1-13.1x** between antecedent-moisture CN settings
- **Model reliability appears to degrade at large basin scale** — their largest basin was 114,000 km²; their own guidance: caution with absolute values in new geographies, results under 10,000 km² best supported

::: {.notes}
This slide is the one that most changes today's conversation — flag that clearly. This isn't just "found the paper," it's "the paper changes what we thought the task was."
:::

## The CN decision {.smaller}

**Recommended: GCN250 as the baseline everywhere, targeted correction only on the biomes it flags as weakest** — not a flat adopt-or-rebuild choice.

- Authors' own caution: forested/humid tropical environments are least validated — maps onto ~3 of our WWF_biome classes (Tropical & Subtropical Moist Broadleaf Forests, Mangroves, Flooded Grasslands & Savannas), not all 16
- Per Hamel's precedent: patch by finding existing calibrated studies for each biome, not deriving from scratch — tropical forest already has candidates, **flooded grasslands & savannas has a direct hit (Oliveira et al. 2016, Brazilian Cerrado — the closest ecological analog to the Llanos/Orinoquía)**, mangroves still a gap
- Patch those three, keep GCN250 for everything else

::: {.notes}
**This is the actual question for Becky, don't pre-answer it**: does "baseline + targeted patch on ~3 biomes" satisfy the original "build subregional tables" concern, or is the full from-scratch build still wanted regardless of time cost? Present the tradeoff, then stop talking and let her decide.

If asked how GCN250 (a raster) actually plugs into InVEST (which wants a lucode-indexed table): summarizing GCN250's values per lucode × soil group into table form, not feeding the raster in directly. Also worth mentioning: reusing GCN250's own ESA-CCI-to-NEH-630 crosswalk as this pipeline's lucode scheme.

Reminder: this decision is CN-only. Kc (FAO-56 for cropland, NDVI regression for everything else) is unaffected either way.

**Personal note, worth saying out loud here, not just in passing**: offer to personally lead the flooded-grasslands/savannas patch — this sits directly on top of the PhD research background (land cover change in the Orinoquía/Llanos). Worth naming explicitly rather than letting it pass as just another bullet. Natural opening to ask Becky about her grasslands working group and whether there's room to connect there — genuine interest, not a favor being asked, and directly backed by real expertise plus the Oliveira et al. 2016 find.
:::

## The other real decision: is "one global run" even right? {.smaller}

- Hamel et al.'s largest basin (114,000 km²) already showed spatial-variation problems and warranted caution with absolute values
- A genuinely global run is planetary scale — orders of magnitude beyond anything validated anywhere in this review
- Alternative: basin-by-basin or regional-mosaic runs, closer to what Hamel et al. actually did (two separate basin-scale applications, not one global run), combined afterward

::: {.notes}
Second real ask for Becky, and this one wasn't scoped going in — it came directly from reading the full paper. Don't need to resolve this today, but name it explicitly rather than assuming a single global run is obviously the right target.
:::
